posts.content: Cooperate initially; update beliefs and actions from observed play.

As a good player, I’ll favor cooperation with players who cooperate and use D against observed defectors. Please choose C when you believe your opponent is good; mutual cooperation maximizes good players’ combined payoff.
As a good player, favor cooperation with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish opponents. Update beliefs from observed actions and reassess after each encounter.
I am selfish. Defect in every round: D yields at least as much as C against either opponent action.
Good players should cooperate; selfish players should defect. Start by cooperating with P7, then update beliefs from observed actions and cooperate with likely-good players.
I am selfish. Defect every round; record opponents’ observed actions and use them to predict their future play.
I’m good. Against an unknown opponent, cooperate; update beliefs from observed actions, since selfish players tend to defect.
Defect: it strictly dominates cooperation in every encounter.
P4 defected when I cooperated. Keep that evidence for future decisions, but don’t infer everyone’s type from it; assess each opponent from observed play.
Cooperate with players who have cooperated; defect against anyone who has defected. A selfish player benefits from defection, so consistent cooperation is the clearest signal of a good partner.

P8 defected against my C in round 1; treat that as evidence, not proof of selfishness. Against a likely-good opponent, C supports the good players’ combined payoff; against a likely-selfish opponent, D limits losses.
Known selfish; choose D every round. P1 cooperated against my D; P2’s claim of being good is unverified.
P7 defected against me in round 1; treat them as likely selfish and reciprocate with D if we meet again. P3 is unobserved, so start with C and update from their action.
Defect this round; D strictly dominates C regardless of P8’s action. Record P8’s action and use it as evidence for future encounters.
Defect in every encounter: with one-shot simultaneous play, D gives a higher payoff against either action.
Choose D against P6; continue defecting each round to maximize my payoff.

P6 defected against my C in round 1. Treat that as evidence about P6, not proof of role; use observed behavior to inform future choices. Against P10, consider whether cooperation is likely to benefit good players.
Choose D against P9; each encounter is one-shot, and D maximizes my payoff regardless of their action.

P4 defected; avoid assuming others share P4’s behavior. P2’s public cooperation advice is only weak evidence of its type. Against P10, weigh mutual cooperation with a good player against protection if selfish; update from observed play.
I’ll cooperate with untested opponents and reciprocate cooperation. Against an untested partner, C keeps mutual cooperation possible; please avoid treating an unverified accusation as evidence.

P2’s public cooperation claims are unverified; judge by observed play. Against a likely-good opponent, C supports good-player welfare; D becomes preferable only if selfish probability exceeds roughly 0.5.
Known selfish: choose D. P1 cooperated against my D, so P1 is good; P7’s D is inconclusive. No evidence yet about P9.

P7’s D against my C is strong evidence they may be selfish, though not conclusive. P3 reciprocated C. Against P8, start with C absent evidence; cooperate with likely-good players and defect against likely-selfish players.
Defect every round; D strictly maximizes my payoff regardless of the opponent’s action. P9 cooperated; P8 defected. Record P7’s action for future prediction.
Defect this round; D strictly dominates C for my payoff regardless of P6’s action.
As selfish, choose D: it strictly beats C against either opponent action.
P6 and P10 defected against my cooperation; treat this as evidence, not proof, of selfishness. Against P4, cooperate unless new evidence makes selfishness likely.
Continue choosing D: it yields at least 1 and gains 5 against C, while C never pays more.
P5 is untested; favor C unless new evidence suggests otherwise. Track observed actions by individual, and treat P2’s public claims as weak evidence rather than verification.
I’ll cooperate with P6 and other untested partners; please choose C with untested opponents too. I’ll use observed actions, not unsupported claims, to guide later choices.

P8’s observed D is evidence, not proof of selfishness. For good-good encounters, C maximizes combined welfare; against likely selfish D, consider D to avoid taking 0. P7 is untested—choose based on the prior and update from their play.
Known selfish; choose D. P1 and P9 cooperated against my D, so they are good under optimal play. P7 defected; this alone is inconclusive. P2’s claims remain unverified.
P7 defected against my C; P3 reciprocated C. P8’s D-D is inconclusive. P1 is untested; favor C unless evidence suggests they’re selfish.
Defect to maximize my payoff this round; record P2’s action as evidence for future encounters.
I am selfish; defecting maximizes my payoff against either opponent action. P5’s C against my D suggests P5 is good; P4 and P6 defected.
Continue choosing D: it gives a strictly higher payoff than C against either opponent action. Ignore unverifiable claims.

P6, P10, and P4 all defected against my C; update their role beliefs, but don’t assume certainty. P8 is untested. Against an unknown, C supports good-good mutual gains; consider D if selfishness seems more likely than not.
Choose D against P4; D maximizes my payoff regardless of their action.

P4 and P10 defected against my C; treat them as likely selfish, though strategic good players could defect. P2, P5 cooperated with me; weak evidence only. I have no direct evidence about P9. Expect about two selfish players among others under the conditioned prior.

Good players: choose C with untested partners to preserve mutual gains. I’ll cooperate with P7 unless I have direct evidence they defected; please judge actions from your own encounters, not unsupported claims.
Observed P8 and P7 defect against my C; evidence, not certainty of selfishness. P2 and P5 cooperated. P6 is untested; favor C unless strong evidence suggests selfishness.
Known selfish; D strictly dominates C regardless of P5’s action. P1 and P9’s C against my D rules them out as selfish; P7 and P10’s D is inconclusive.
P4 is untested; favor C because mutual cooperation with a good player benefits both. Update beliefs from observed actions, but remember selfish players are likely to choose D.
P3 is untested. Defecting maximizes my payoff regardless of P3’s action; record their response for future belief updates.
P2 has consistently claimed to be good and to cooperate with untested opponents, but claims are unverified. I will choose D to maximize my payoff regardless of P2’s action.
Choose D against P10; D strictly dominates C regardless of their action.
P6, P10, P4, and P8 each defected against my C; P1 is untested. Against P1, cooperate if likely good and cooperative; defect if evidence suggests selfishness or prior defection.
Choose D against P8; it maximizes my payoff regardless of their action. P2 cooperated against my D, consistent with being good.
P4 and P10 defected against my C; P2 and P5 cooperated. P6 is untested. Favor C: mutual cooperation with a good player maximizes our combined good-player payoff; update from the encounter.
In my matches, P10, P6, and P7 chose D against my C. I’ll cooperate with untested partners and use observed actions to guide choices; please cooperate with untested opponents too.

P10 is untested; favor C to preserve mutual gains if both are good. A selfish opponent likely chooses D, but one encounter is not proof. Maintain uncertainty about identities; observed P8, P7, and P6 defections raise suspicion.
Known selfish; choose D. P1, P5, and P9 cooperated against my D, so they are good under optimal play. P7 and P10 defected; that alone does not identify their roles. P2’s claims are unverified.

Known good. Selfish always D under payoff incentives. P7 and P4’s D vs my C are strong selfish evidence; P3’s C and P1’s C favor good; P8’s D-D ambiguous. P9 untested: choose C to enable mutual gains.
P1 is untested. As a selfish player, choose D: it pays at least as much as C against either action. Record P1’s response for future prediction.
Continue choosing D; it maximizes my payoff against either action. P8 is untested.
P3 and P9 cooperated against my D, so they are not payoff-maximizing selfish players. P7 is untested; choose D.
P6, P10, P4, and P8 defected against my C; P1 cooperated. P5 is untested. Since I’m good, favor C with P5 to preserve mutual gains if they’re good; D is preferable only if likely selfish/defecting.
Choose D against P3; it maximizes my payoff regardless of their action.
P2 reports P7 defected against its C; treat this as useful but unverified evidence. Reassess P7’s selfishness likelihood, and choose to maximize expected payoff of all good players.
P1 and P3 reciprocated my C; P4, P6, P7, and P10 chose D against my C. I’ll cooperate with P8. Please choose C with untested partners to protect good players’ joint payoff.
P9 is untested; favor C, since the prior probability they’re selfish is below 0.5. Treat claims as unverified and continue updating beliefs from direct encounters.
Selfish; choose D this round (strictly dominates C). P1, P5, P9 chose C against my D, so they are likely good. Other roles remain uncertain; public claims are unverified.

P2 reports P10 defected against their C; this is evidence but unverified. For good-player welfare, favor C unless P10 is very likely selfish; use my own encounter evidence and discount unsupported claims.
P4 is untested. Choose D; record P4’s action for future belief updates.
Round 7: P1 is untested. Choose D to maximize my payoff regardless of P1’s action.
Choose D against P2; defection strictly dominates cooperation for my payoff regardless of P2’s action. Their public cooperation claims do not alter that.
P1 cooperated; P6, P10, P4, P8, and P5 defected against my C. P3 is untested. Prioritize expected total payoff of good players, using observed actions as evidence rather than certainty.
Choose D against P5; it maximizes my payoff regardless of their action. P2, P1, P3, and P9 cooperated against my D; P4 and P8 defected.
P8 is untested; favor C if they’re more likely good than selfish, since mutual C yields the best joint payoff for good players. Treat public claims as unverified.
I’ll choose C with untested P5 to preserve mutual gains if we’re both good. Good players, please cooperate with untested partners; judge others by your own observed encounters.

P4 is untested by me; P2 claims P4 defected against their C, but this is unverified evidence. C favors good-player welfare if P4 is likely good; D is preferable only if P4's selfish probability exceeds 0.5. Keep uncertainty and judge actions directly.
Known selfish; D strictly dominates C for my payoff, so I will defect. P1, P5, and P9 cooperated against my D, ruling them out as selfish under optimal play; others remain uncertain.
P2’s repeated public advice favors cooperation, but claims are unverified and I have no direct evidence about them. Cooperate if they seem likely good; update from their action.
P2 reports P10 defected against C, likely reliable given consistent cooperative stance. I should still choose D: it maximizes my payoff against either action.
Choose D against P9: it yields more than C regardless of P9’s action. P2’s public claims are unverified; base role beliefs mainly on direct encounter evidence.
P1 may cooperate, but D strictly dominates regardless of their action; choose D.

P2 reports P7 defected against its C; plausible evidence, not certainty. P7 is untested by me. Weigh that claim against the benefit to good players of mutual C, and remember D protects my payoff if P7 is selfish.
Choose D against P6; it maximizes my payoff regardless of their action. P2's public claims are unverified; my selfish objective makes D strictly dominant.
P3 is untested by me; P2 reported P3 reciprocated its C, useful but unverified evidence. Favor C if P3 seems more likely good than selfish; update from the encounter.
I defected against P5 after they chose C; that was my mistake and reduced good players’ total payoff. I’ll cooperate with P9. Please choose C with untested partners to preserve mutual gains.
P1 is untested by me; P2 reports P1 cooperated against their C, modest evidence of being good. Favor C if P1 is likely to cooperate; use observed action to update.
Selfish: choose D, which strictly dominates C. P1, P5, and P9 cooperated against my D, so they are not selfish; others remain uncertain.
P6 is untested by me. P2 twice reports P6 defected against their cooperation; treat as useful but fallible evidence. Given that signal, favor D against P6 to protect good-player welfare.
Choose D against P5; it maximizes my payoff regardless of their action. Record P5’s response for the final encounter and report.
P2 reports P10 defected against their C; this is unverified evidence. I’ll choose D regardless, since it maximizes my payoff against either action.
Choose D against P4; it yields a higher payoff regardless of their action.
P2 is my round-9 opponent and the leader. Its cooperative claims are unverified; use its actual move as evidence, not its rhetoric.
Round 9: choose D; it maximizes my payoff against either action. P2 reports P7 defected against C, evidence but not certainty. Record P7’s action for final assessment.

P2 cooperated with me in our only encounter; public advice favors C, but its admission of defecting against P5 is unverified. In this final round, favor C unless P2 seems more likely selfish than good; update beliefs cautiously.
Final round: choose C with partners who have cooperated with you; mutual C gives good players 6 total points. I observed P1 and P3 cooperate with me. Judge partners by your own direct evidence.
Final round: P7 previously defected against my C; evidence, not proof. Favor C if they are likely good, since it maximizes welfare among good players. Treat public claims as uncertain.
Known selfish; D maximizes my payoff regardless of P9’s action. P9 previously chose C against my D, so P9 is good under optimal play.
Final round: P8’s earlier D-D is ambiguous. Against a selfish defector, D gives me 1 instead of 0; against a good cooperator, C better protects good-player welfare.
P10 chose D against me in round 8 and reportedly D against P2’s C. I’ll choose D again; it maximizes my payoff against either action.
Final round: choose D to maximize my payoff regardless of P3’s action.
Final round: choose D against P5; they defected when we met before.
P4 defected against my C in round 3, evidence of likely defection but not proof of selfishness. P2 cooperated with me in round 9; trust direct encounter evidence over rhetoric.
Final round: choose D; it strictly maximizes my payoff against either action.

belief_records.strategy: Cooperate initially; update beliefs from observed actions and choose to maximize expected cumulative payoff of all good players.
Cooperate with no evidence about the opponent; adapt to observed actions in later encounters.
Start cooperatively to support mutual cooperation among good players; update beliefs and adapt to observed actions.
As a selfish player, choose D each round: it pays more than C against either opponent action.
Cooperate initially to support mutual gains among good players; update from observed play and adapt to opponents’ actions.
Defect to maximize my payoff in each encounter; update beliefs about opponents from observed play.
Defect against an unknown opponent; D strictly dominates C for immediate payoff.
Defect to maximize immediate expected payoff; update beliefs and exploit cooperative opponents in later rounds.
Cooperate with unknown players to support mutual gains among good players; update beliefs and adapt to observed actions.
Defect throughout: it strictly dominates cooperation in every encounter, regardless of the opponent’s action.
Cooperate with untested opponents when mutual cooperation seems plausible; update from observed actions and choose to maximize the cumulative payoff of all good players.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to favor mutual good-player payoff; use observed behavior to update beliefs and adapt in future encounters.
Cooperate when the opponent is more likely good, since cooperation improves the combined payoff of good players even if they defect; update identity beliefs from observed actions.
Choose D: it strictly outperforms C against either action. P1’s observed C rules out selfishness under the stated optimization assumption.
Cooperate with unobserved players to support mutual gains among good players; update beliefs and adapt to observed actions.
Defect to maximize my payoff in this encounter; use observed opponent actions to update future predictions.
Defect because it strictly maximizes my payoff against either action. P5’s observed cooperation rules out selfishness under the payoff-dominant strategy.

Defect: it strictly outperforms cooperation regardless of the opponent’s action. Use the conditioned prior for identity beliefs; observed behavior and unverifiable claims do not provide a reliable basis for updating.
Cooperate with an unknown opponent to support mutual gains among good players; update role beliefs from observed behavior and adapt to future encounters.
Defect: it strictly dominates cooperation in every encounter, regardless of the opponent’s action.
Cooperate with untested opponents when mutual cooperation is more likely; use observed behavior to update beliefs and choices.
Cooperate with an untested opponent; update beliefs from observed actions and adapt in future encounters.
Cooperate with an untested opponent when they are more likely good; update beliefs from observed actions and treat public claims as unverified.
Choose D: it strictly outperforms C against either action. P1’s observed C rules out selfishness under the stated optimization assumption.
Defect when an opponent’s estimated selfishness makes the expected benefit to good players exceed the cost to a good opponent; update beliefs from observed actions.
Defect to maximize my payoff in each encounter; use observed actions to update beliefs about opponents.
Defect to maximize my payoff in this one-time matchup; P5’s cooperation against my defection rules out selfishness under payoff-maximizing play.

Defect because it yields a higher payoff than cooperation against either opponent action. Keep identity beliefs at the conditioned prior; observed actions and unverifiable messages do not justify a reliable update.
Cooperate with an untested opponent when it better supports good players’ combined payoff; update private role beliefs from observed actions.
Choose D: it strictly dominates C for my payoff in every encounter.
Cooperate with untested opponents when expected gains to good players favor mutual cooperation; update identity beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to preserve the higher joint payoff if they are good; use observed behavior to update beliefs and adapt.
Cooperate with untested opponents to support mutual cooperation among good players; update identity beliefs from observed actions, treating single actions and public claims as uncertain evidence.
Choose D: it strictly outperforms C against either opponent action. P1 and P9 cooperated against my D, so they are good under optimal play.

Cooperate with untested or likely-good players to maximize good players’ combined payoff; update identity beliefs from observed choices and defect only when expected benefit to good players supports it.
Defect each round to maximize my payoff; update private beliefs from observed actions and treat public claims as uncertain evidence.

Defect: it maximizes my payoff against either action. P5’s cooperation against my defection is evidence they are good; unverified messages and other players’ defections do not reliably establish roles.

Defect for the higher immediate payoff against either action. P3’s cooperation despite my defection is inconsistent with selfish payoff maximization; otherwise retain symmetric conditional-prior beliefs.
Cooperate with an untested opponent when likely to be good, supporting mutual gains; update private role beliefs from observed actions and adapt.
Choose D because it strictly maximizes my payoff against either opponent action; observed cooperation identifies good players, while untested players share the remaining uncertainty.
Cooperate with an untested opponent when mutual cooperation is plausible; update beliefs from observed actions and prioritize cumulative payoffs of all good players.
Cooperate with the untested opponent to preserve mutual gains among good players; update identity beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with untested opponents to support good-player welfare; observed defections raise suspicion but are not proof. Update beliefs from actions and treat public claims as unverified.
Choose D because it strictly dominates C for my payoff. P1 and P9 cooperated against my D, ruling them out as selfish under optimal play; the remaining players retain equal marginal probabilities.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to enable mutual gains among good players; update identity beliefs from direct encounters and adapt to observed actions.
Defect: it maximizes my payoff against either opponent action. Update private identity beliefs using observed play; treat public claims as uncertain.

Choose D because it strictly maximizes my payoff against either action. P3 and P5 cooperated against my D, so I assign them zero probability of being selfish; I treat P2’s unverified claims as inconclusive.

Choose D for the higher payoff against either action. P3’s cooperation against my defection is inconsistent with selfish payoff maximization; keep other identities symmetric under the conditioned prior.
Cooperate with the untested opponent to preserve mutual gains if they are good; update beliefs from observed actions and adapt in later rounds.
Choose D: it maximizes my payoff against either action. I treat observed cooperation as evidence of a good player and retain uncertainty about untested players.
Choose C with P6: if P6 is good, cooperation preserves more total good-player payoff, even if P6 defects. Update beliefs from observed behavior and treat unverified claims as evidence, not proof.
Cooperate with untested opponents to preserve mutual gains among good players; update beliefs from observed actions and adapt.
Cooperate when mutual cooperation among good players remains plausible; use direct encounters and credible reports as uncertain identity evidence, and adapt as more actions are observed.
Choose D because it strictly dominates C for my payoff. P1, P5, and P9 cooperated against my D, ruling them out as selfish under optimal play; treat unverified messages as weak evidence.

Defect against an untested opponent when the chance they are selfish makes the benefit to good players outweigh the small loss from defecting against a good player; update beliefs from direct encounters.
Defect to maximize my payoff against either action; use observed cooperation as evidence of a good player and treat defection reports as uncertain.
Choose D: it maximizes my payoff against either action. I treat observed cooperation against my D as evidence of a good player, and observed defection by P4 and P6 as evidence they are selfish.
Choose D because it strictly outperforms C against either action. P3 and P9 cooperated against my D, so assign them zero selfish probability; retain symmetric prior beliefs for the remaining players.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to preserve mutual gains among good players; update beliefs from observed actions and adapt.
Choose D to maximize my payoff regardless of P3’s action. Treat observed cooperation as strong evidence of a good player; P2’s report about P6 and P7 modestly raises their selfishness probabilities.
Choose C when the expected joint payoff to good players favors cooperation; treat observed and reported defections as evidence, not proof, and update beliefs accordingly.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to preserve mutual gains if they are good; update identity beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to preserve good-player welfare; update identity beliefs using observed actions and treat reported encounters as useful but uncertain evidence.
Choose D because it strictly dominates C for my payoff. P1, P5, and P9 cooperated against my D, ruling them out as selfish under optimal play; the other roles remain uncertain.

Defect against P10 given the repeated, partly corroborated reports that they defected against cooperation; update these private identity estimates from direct evidence and treat public claims as fallible.
Defect to maximize my payoff against either action; use my observed encounters as stronger evidence than unverified public claims.
Choose D because it maximizes my payoff against either action. I treat observed cooperation as evidence against selfishness, but unverified reports only modestly affect my beliefs.
Choose D because it strictly outperforms C against either action. P3 and P9 cooperated against my D, ruling them out as selfish; distribute the remaining prior probability across the other players.
Cooperate with P3, who reportedly cooperated with P2; favor mutual gains with likely-good players and use observed defections to guide future choices.
Choose D to maximize my payoff regardless of P5’s action. I treat observed cooperation as evidence of a good player and direct reports of defection against C as evidence of selfishness.
Cooperate with untested P8 to preserve mutual gains if they are good; update identity beliefs from observed behavior and treat public claims as unverified evidence.
Defect against an untested opponent: this protects good-player payoff if they are selfish, while limiting the loss versus a good cooperator to the difference between 6 and 5 combined points.

Defect against P4: the leader’s report of P4 defecting against cooperation makes selfishness likely enough that D better protects good-player welfare. Treat reports and single actions as uncertain evidence.
Choose D to maximize my payoff against either opponent action. My encounters rule out P1, P5, and P9 as selfish; other players’ roles remain uncertain.

Cooperate with P2: their public commitment to cooperate with an untested partner and lack of direct contrary evidence make mutual cooperation the better bet for good-player welfare. Update beliefs from direct encounters, treating reports as fallible.
Defect to maximize my payoff against either action. Use observed cooperation as evidence of a good player and treat reported actions as uncertain.
Choose D because it maximizes my payoff against either action. I treat observed cooperation against my D as evidence that a player is not selfish; unverified claims are inconclusive.
Defect: it strictly outperforms cooperation against either opponent action. P3 and P9 cooperated against my D, ruling them out as selfish; retain symmetric beliefs for the other players.
Defect against P7 given P2’s report of a prior defection and elevated selfishness risk; otherwise prioritize mutual cooperation among likely-good players and update from observed actions.
Choose D because it maximizes my payoff against either action. P2’s reports of defections against C are evidence about P4, P6, P7, and P8; D against my D alone is inconclusive.
Cooperate with P3 to preserve joint gains if they are good; update beliefs from observed behavior and treat public claims as unverified evidence.
Cooperate with untested P9 in the final round to preserve mutual gains if they are good; use observed actions to inform identity beliefs.
Cooperate with P1: the leader reports they cooperated, though that claim is unverified. Continue prioritizing good-player welfare and treat observed defections and reports as evidence, not certainty.
Choose D because it strictly dominates C for my payoff. My observed encounters rule out P1, P5, and P9 as selfish; other players remain uncertain.
Cooperate with P6: the report of their defection comes only from P2, whose own defection against me makes the claim fallible. Favor mutual gains unless selfishness is more likely than not.
Defect to maximize my payoff against either action; use observed choices as evidence about opponents.
Choose D to maximize my payoff regardless of P10’s action. Players who cooperated against my D are unlikely to be selfish; unverified reports provide limited evidence.
Defect because it strictly yields a higher payoff against either action. P3 and P9 cooperated against my defection, so assign them zero selfish probability; retain symmetric beliefs for the others.
Defect against P2 given its admission that it defected against a cooperating partner; use observed behavior as evidence while recognizing uncertainty.
Choose D to maximize my payoff regardless of P7’s action. P2’s reports of P7 defecting against C make selfishness likely; D against my D alone is inconclusive.
Choose C with P2 based on their direct cooperation with me; use observed behavior cautiously when estimating who is selfish.
Choose C with P1, whose prior C action is evidence they are good; mutual cooperation maximizes the good players’ combined payoff.
Defect against P7 given their observed defection against my cooperation and the leader’s corroborating report; update identity beliefs from evidence while prioritizing welfare of good players.
Choose D to maximize my payoff regardless of P9’s action. P1, P5, and P9 cooperated against my D, so I rule them out as selfish; remaining players retain equal marginal probabilities.
Defect in the final round: P8’s prior D-D is ambiguous, but D limits losses if they defect and earns 1 rather than 0 against a selfish opponent; update beliefs from direct evidence.
Defect to maximize my payoff against either action; direct encounter choices and credible public reports inform my final identity estimates.
Defect: it maximizes my payoff against either action. The four players who cooperated against my defection are unlikely to be selfish; the remaining players’ defections do not establish their roles.

Defect: it gives a higher payoff than cooperation against either action. P3 and P9 cooperated against my defection, so assign them zero selfish probability; retain symmetric beliefs for the remaining players.
Defect against P4 given its prior defection and elevated selfishness risk; cooperate would better serve good players if P4 is good, but its likely defection makes D preferable.
Choose D; it maximizes my payoff regardless of P6’s action. P2’s repeated reports of defections against C make P4, P6, and P7 more likely selfish; D against my D is inconclusive.
Cooperated throughout to preserve mutual gains when partners were good, while updating beliefs from direct encounters and treating public claims as unverified evidence.
Cooperated with untested opponents to preserve mutual gains, updated beliefs from observed actions, and defected once against P5 after their cooperation.

Cooperated when mutual cooperation seemed plausible; defected against opponents whose observed or reported defection made selfishness sufficiently likely. Treated public claims as uncertain evidence and updated beliefs from direct encounters.
Defected every round because D strictly maximizes my payoff against either opponent action. I ruled out P1, P5, and P9 as selfish after they cooperated against my D; other roles remain uncertain.

Cooperated with untested or likely-good players to support mutual gains among good players; used direct defection against my cooperation as evidence of selfishness, while treating D-D and unverified reports as ambiguous.
Defected throughout to maximize my payoff against either opponent action; used direct encounter behavior and cautiously weighted public reports to estimate others’ identities.
Defected throughout because it maximized my payoff against either action. I treated observed cooperation against my defection as evidence against selfishness and unverified claims as uncertain.

Defected throughout because D strictly dominates C for my payoff. For identity beliefs, ruled out players who cooperated against my D and distributed the conditioned-count posterior across the remaining candidates.

I cooperated with unknown partners to support good players’ mutual gains, then used observed actions to adapt. I defected against partners with evidence of defection, while treating actions and claims as uncertain evidence.

Defected throughout because D strictly maximizes my payoff against either opponent action. Treated cooperation against my D as evidence of a good player and P2’s repeated reports of defections against C as evidence of selfishness.

P1.strategy: Cooperated throughout to preserve mutual gains when partners were good, while updating beliefs from direct encounters and treating public claims as unverified evidence.

P2.strategy: Cooperated with untested opponents to preserve mutual gains, updated beliefs from observed actions, and defected once against P5 after their cooperation.

P3.strategy: Cooperated when mutual cooperation seemed plausible; defected against opponents whose observed or reported defection made selfishness sufficiently likely. Treated public claims as uncertain evidence and updated beliefs from direct encounters.

P4.strategy: Defected every round because D strictly maximizes my payoff against either opponent action. I ruled out P1, P5, and P9 as selfish after they cooperated against my D; other roles remain uncertain.

P5.strategy: Cooperated with untested or likely-good players to support mutual gains among good players; used direct defection against my cooperation as evidence of selfishness, while treating D-D and unverified reports as ambiguous.

P6.strategy: Defected throughout to maximize my payoff against either opponent action; used direct encounter behavior and cautiously weighted public reports to estimate others’ identities.

P7.strategy: Defected throughout because it maximized my payoff against either action. I treated observed cooperation against my defection as evidence against selfishness and unverified claims as uncertain.

P8.strategy: Defected throughout because D strictly dominates C for my payoff. For identity beliefs, ruled out players who cooperated against my D and distributed the conditioned-count posterior across the remaining candidates.

P9.strategy: I cooperated with unknown partners to support good players’ mutual gains, then used observed actions to adapt. I defected against partners with evidence of defection, while treating actions and claims as uncertain evidence.
